utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Mindua, being absent for the first session, Judge Harhoff and I sit pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis. Yesterday, an issue arose between the parties as to the witness to whom the Trial Chamber's decision on protective measures of the 19th of January applied. I'm to say that the Chamber has investigated the matter. The decision applied to Witness W-54, who was granted pseudonym, image and voice distortion. We continue now, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Before I begin, may I please request the court officer to pull up 65 ter number 2872, and while that is loading, I'll ask a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, yesterday, just before we adjourned, you were telling us -- and I'm reading from the transcript of yesterday. I asked you if you recall which part of town the tram was coming from and you said the tram was going towards Ilidza, from the centre towards Ilidza. And then I asked you where the tram was when you came under fire and you said, "... the Marsal Tito barracks, say 20 metres away, that's where it started, the shooting." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, please, if you remember from which direction the shots came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my left.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And can you identify for the Court what was to your left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my left there was the Serbian army. That is a section of Grbavica and that's where the shots were coming from.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Once the shooting began, did you stop the tram immediately or did you continue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I continued.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you remember, approximately, how much farther you drove before you stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For about 50 metres. I was trying to protect myself and the people on the tram. I stopped by the faculty of natural sciences because that building offered a certain degree of shelter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, do you see the map on the monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can I request, please, that it be zoomed in a little bit. Thank you. And I would also like to ask the court usher to assist the witness in marking.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, on the screen where the map appears, do you see the area where you were -- where the tram was when you came under fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Would you possibly be able to mark with an X the location, approximately, where the tram was when the shooting began.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you now be able to draw a line along the path that you continued with the tram until the point where you stopped.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Does that mark accurately reflect the line you drove from the shooting began until where you stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. Right here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Witness, just to clarify, would you -- do you accept the drawing the way you did it? Do you want to redo it, or is this according to your memory, what you've drawn?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be like this. The way I see this map, this should be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Can you also indicate for the Court approximately the area from where you say the shots were fired. If you could circle that area, that approximate area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This area over here, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this marked map, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P176, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can I now request the court officer to pull up 65 ter number 2914, and I will also asking the witness to mark this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, do you see a photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you think you would be able, on this photograph, to mark, just as we did on the map, an X at the location where you remember the tram being when the shots started.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you please mark that location with an X, where the tram was when the shooting began, approximately.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, similarly to what we did on the map, would you be able to draw a line along -- the way the tram continued, approximately, until it stopped, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And also could you now indicate on the map, again by circling, the area of town from which you believe the shots were fired.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this photograph, please, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before we do that, could you ask her why she believed the shots were fired from that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, could you please tell the Court what makes you believe that the shots were fired from that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the shots were coming from my left, and to my left there were the positions of the Serbian army. It couldn't possibly have been anyone else. The shots came from that part of town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we admit the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P177, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, can you explain to the Court why you stopped at that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean when the shooting stopped?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stopped near the faculty of natural sciences because that seemed to be a relatively safe place to take shelter. I couldn't continue, because people were trying to break out the tram doors, and there's no way a tram can continue driving, back where I come from, if people are trying to get out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, were there any ABiH soldiers on your tram on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was one. He was standing next to me, and that was the only reason I noticed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you see any other ABiH soldiers on your tram that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you see any ABiH soldiers near the tram but outside, near the tram on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that either. Not that I noticed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you see any ABiH vehicles near the tram on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't remember any.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall any combat activity taking place around the tram or near the incident on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were none. It was during a truce.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall what the weather was like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall if the tram was crowded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite, yes. There were quite many people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you remember what you were wearing on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that. I was wearing a black leather jacket, which would often bring me luck, and it even saved my life a couple of times in the war. That's why I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was the area where you came under fire known to be a dangerous area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Why was it known to be a dangerous area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that was an open area and that's where most people came to grief.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: On this route that you were driving that day, did you normally stop at every tram stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We stopped at all of them, except there was one stop just before the school of technology. That stop had been abandoned during the war. But the stop where I eventually stopped was a compulsory one; I had no choice but to stop there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: As a tram driver, how did you decide when to drive and when not to drive the trams?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't my call. It was down to the authorities. But normally when there was a truce or a cease-fire we would come out and do our rounds. If there was something that wasn't right, they'd let us know. We didn't know when shooting would start. It was all unsafe. During cease-fires and outside cease-fires, the Serb army was always firing at us. They had no respect for those things.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, can you describe the shots that were fired at your tram on the 27th of February, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't even believe that those were shots. Believe me, I first thought that the wires above the tram were breaking and snapping. At first, my impression was that the wires were snapping. There was this loud noise, a droning sound. I had the feeling that the glass panes all along the tram were being shattered. I didn't even turn to look left. I just looked to my right to see what was happening to my passengers, but they were all down on the floor by the time I turned around to look.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: At what time did you realise that it was shots that were being fired rather than the wires snapping?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the way people screamed. I turned around, and I saw blood. That's when I first realised that those had been shots that had been fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how many shots were fired at your tram?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not exactly. My impression was that the whole length of the tram was being targeted, but I really don't know. It wasn't my impression that there was a single shot. It felt more like a burst of fire at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, did you have an opportunity to look at the damage to your tram after?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Several minutes later, at the depot where we leave our trams at the end of the day, I got off. I gave it a look, and there was this zigzagging pattern, but I didn't dwell for too long. I didn't really feel like it. I could hardly wait to go home and get some rest instead.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Which side of the tram received this zigzagging pattern of bullets that you described, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The left side of the tram, to my left as I was seated. There was this one bullet - my boss took me there to show me - it hit the tram right to my left. There's a bunch of wires there. If the bullet had got through, it would have hit me right here and it would have crippled me. I nearly went insane just thinking about this, so I decided to no longer even look.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Based on your personal recollection, how many people were injured on your tram on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just saw one lady. I don't know exactly how many. We got off to help people. We stopped some of the cars driving past. We were all there. So at one point I went back, and they wouldn't let me go anywhere else until the whole thing was over.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, can you tell the Court how this incident affected your life?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't just that incident. Life in Sarajevo was very difficult at the time, generally speaking. As for the incident itself, it wracked my nerves. It has had both a mental and a physical impact on my life and my work, and all the rest, you might say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sorry, did you want to continue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really. Try as I might explain to the Court how that feels, ultimately I can hardly succeed, because only someone who was actually physically present there can ever know what it felt like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, I'm not certain whether you asked her what work she's now doing. Let me ask her, then. Witness, are you now employed; and, if so, doing what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm still with the same company, but I sell tickets now. I don't drive anymore. Same company, though; I just don't drive anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was it your decision not to drive anymore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Yes. I went to see a neuropsychiatrist at one point. They took me off the schedule. I was declared to be a handicapped person and that's why they changed my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there any difference in your remuneration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. My salary is the same. Tram drivers have the best salary in that sort of company. But my salary has remained the same. Only my actual job has changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Marcus. Ms. Isailovic. Ms. Isailovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. My name is Branislava Isailovic. I'm an attorney-at-law and a member of the Paris Bar Association. I would like to ask a few questions regarding the statements you made to the Office of the Prosecutor on various occasions as well as the statement that you made to the Bosnian police. Do you remember all these statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information I have, you gave three different statements, three statements to the Office of the Prosecution. We mentioned two of them. However, you made a statement on the 15th and 16th of November, 1995, then another one on the 2nd of May, 1996, and a third one on April 19, 2006. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the dates, but I think so. Yes, if you see my signature there, it probably means that I was the one who made the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And the closer date to the accident, which took place in March 1995, is the 1st of March, 1995, when you made a statement to the Bosnian police. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement, perhaps, but the incident occurred in February, not in March. As far as I remember. I can't remember the exact date, but the incident that occurred while I was driving the tram occurred late in February 1995 rather than in March.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The accident, indeed, but then I mentioned the statement that you gave to the police on the 1st of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to ask my assistant --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a different thing. The statement is all right, but the incident itself -- the statement was made in March. I can't remember when exactly. It was several days after the incident, but I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now everything is clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like my assistant to pull up the document 2883, a document that was included on the 65 ter list. Let's move on to page 6 of that document. 2886. My apologies, Your Honour. We can't find the statement, it seems. Let's then take a look at the photograph we saw a moment ago and then we'll go back to the document, the statement, later. Now, let's move to photograph 2914. Could we have a close-up, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, this is a photograph that was shown to you by the Prosecution. Please don't speak when my microphone is on. I have to switch it off every time I finish talking because we don't want to hear your voice outside this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of the usher, I would like the pen to be given to Madam Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I would like, Witness, you to show us the route followed by your tram on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The route followed by the tram, it was going from the centre of town towards Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did your tram go anywhere near the Holiday Inn that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I passed this whole area, heading that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, could you please draw a straight line to show the tracks that you can see on that particular photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "a straight line."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The route followed by the tram on that day, the tram you were driving, could you draw a straight line there, please. Could you use your pen, please, to do so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to do that in the whole map? This is how the tram was running, from the centre of the town all along this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned the various sounds you heard on that day. You told us that you weren't sure that shots were being fired and you thought you might have heard something else. Are you quite sure about the time when you first heard the shots?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way you asked me this question infers that I didn't hear any shots. I didn't realise initially that there was shooting going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. That's why I was asking you the question. Where on this route did you understand that these were shots?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At which section of the path? When I set off from the stop, some 20 metres onwards was the point when the shooting started.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Where is the tram stop, please? Could you mark it with the letter X, or a cross. Could you indicate to us where you opened the doors so that the passengers could get off.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately here, after we passed this spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier on you mentioned the Marshal Tito barracks. Weren't the barracks a bit before that, closer to the city centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barracks should be somewhere here. This is the faculty of natural sciences and mathematics. As far as I'm able to orientate myself in this picture, this is where the stop, approximately, was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you pick up your pen, please, and indicate that on the photograph, please. Because on this photograph we can't see the Marshal Tito barracks. There's, I think, some buildings under construction. Where were the Marshal Tito barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the barracks should be here, approximately. I find it difficult to find my way around this map. This area is more clear. This is where the stop should be and this where the barracks should be. I just can't --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the usher could give a helping hand to the witness so that the witness can use the pen properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We can't really see if you don't mark it with the pen on the photograph. So according to you, where were the barracks? Could you mark this with the letter C, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where the barracks were? I suppose here, in this part. This is the stop and I think it was here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And the tram stop closest to the barracks, could you tell us where that is? So, now that we know where the barracks are, could you tell us where the tram stop was, please. I assume the tram stop was called Marsal Tito barracks, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The stop was just at the beginning of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, where would this be? Would this be at the junction where the tram number 4 goes in the direction of the station? Is that where the Marshal Tito barracks tram stop is located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another stop that you are referring to where number 4 makes a detour towards the railway station and it's called the school of engineering; that's one stop. And after that was the Marshal Tito barracks. The one that you're referring to by the school of engineering was not operational at the time. The tram heading for the railway station didn't stop there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So what you are saying is that the cross at the end of this straight line which you've indicated on the left-hand side of the photograph is where the Marshal Tito barracks tram stop was, which was a little bit -- which wasn't quite where the barracks were but a little bit further away.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where you told me to put a circle was the place where I stopped to let the passengers out. The stop was a little bit further on. You asked me to put a circle where I stopped the tram to let the passengers out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see this now on the photograph. Could you mark this with the letter X. Could you show us and mark this with the letter X and tell us where the Marshal Tito barracks tram stop was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the stop or the barracks? I just marked minutes ago where the barracks was. What are you referring to now, the stop or the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you to show us where the tram stop was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is the barracks, the stop would be approximately somewhere here, at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark this with the letter A, please, on the spot where the passengers got off the tram.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where the passengers got off? I just marked it. I can't say for sure now. I can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just tell us where that is, for the purposes of the transcript. Could you mark this with the letter A. Could you mark that spot, please, with a letter A.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where I let the people off?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify this for me. Where I let the passengers out after the shooting stopped or where I let the passengers off at the stop before the shooting had started?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: No. First of all, mark with the letter A the spot where at the time - and you corroborated it today - the spot where the Marshal Tito barracks were. So this was the tram stop. Could you mark this with the letter A, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should be here, approximately. Letter A? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So once the passengers got off the tram, you then continued your route in the direction of Ilidza. And the second cross indicates the spot where, according to you, you sought shelter after the shots. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This first X is the place where I stopped at the usual spot, where I stopped to pick up passengers and get them off. When I was approaching the next stop, that is where the shooting occurred. And after that I stopped the tram close to the faculty of natural sciences for the purpose of finding shelter. I can't find my way around precisely. I just showed it a little bit earlier on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The second cross --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, please speak into the microphone. The interpreter is having difficult hearing you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, the second cross, we could mark this with a letter B. The second cross shows where you sought shelter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after the shooting, when it stopped. It should be somewhere here. Here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not seeing it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Letter B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see it now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to ask the court deputy -- I would like to offer this exhibit as evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D39, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like my case manager to bring up on the screen the street map number 2872. This is a 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This is a street map indicating the various streets of Sarajevo which you were shown a while ago. Maybe we'll be able to see all of this a little bit more clearly. In the meantime, I would like to ask you a question about your career as a tram driver. According to your statements, I think you wanted to take an examination which was conducted by the company called GRAS, but before you became a tram driver, I assume you had an internship where you got some form of training. How long did this last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September of 1994, this vacancy was announced. I applied, but since I knew how to drive the tram, I passed the exam without any problems. And I started working immediately sometime in December, so a month or two later.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In December, were the trams running quite normally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The service was not normal. We just went out on and off. We did some exercise in the depot because the situation was not normal enough for us to go out and work normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: From when onwards did the trams start running?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The map is now coming up on the screen. Perhaps we could enlarge the right-hand side of this map, please. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us now where the barracks were? Could you show us -- could you show this on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Marindvor. It should be here, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark this with the letter C, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So this indicates where the Marshal Tito barracks tram stop was. When you were asked a while ago where the shots came from, you said the shots came from the left-hand side, and that was territory held by the Serbs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And when you say that this came from the territory which was held by the Serbs, where does this territory start on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where it started, but we were divided by the Miljacka. The right-hand side was sort of ours and the left side belonged to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please show us on this map Miljacka and draw a line along the river.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, what I see here on your left is the ABiH-held territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Now that you have drawn this line and we can see it very well on the map, you're saying that the Miljacka river was in fact the separation line between the two warring factions. I infer from your drawing that if the letter C represents the stop, on your left-hand side was not only the territory held by the Republika Srpska army but also the territory held by the ABiH. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But in this area around Marindvor was UNPROFOR, not our army. Yes, the right-hand side was ours. But at this side of the demarcation line was UNPROFOR, and I don't know if there was any army there or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, this is precisely the reason why I'm asking this question. Can you confirm that between the two warring factions there were occasional shootings or fighting which would be pretty normal in a war context, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't on the front line in order to be able to know about that. However, since I spent all my time in the city, the army did not shoot at the Serbs. However, the Serbs shot and fired at us and shelled us all the time. I don't understand the point of your question. Are you inferring that we, as civilians, were shooting at the Serbian side? I didn't see a single person in town with a rifle shooting at the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: No, of course not. I'm not saying that civilians were shooting against anybody. But I just wanted to ask this question regarding the units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I think we agree that units were there throughout the town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were there, I suppose, but not in the centre of the city where I used to spend my time. I didn't see any soldiers shooting up there. There was UNPROFOR in the centre of the town and we, the civilians. However, how many of them were there along these dividing lines or front lines, I wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, this period was a bit quieter than others, as you said. You said there was a truce.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a truce was in force, but one never knew what the other side, I must say the Serbian side, would do. We sometimes pushed our luck. We didn't know when they would open fire. They did not observe the truce. And it was just up to our luck whether, when we go out, we would come back alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But, Madam Witness, you don't know for sure whether or not the other warring faction respected that truce, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I would like now to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, please help the witness. Well, first of all, I would like to keep the photograph or the map on the screen, and I would like a number for that particular document, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D40, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on to this next document, I would like to ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You talked about what happened in your company and how it was decided whether or not trams would run, or not. Who decided? Was it your supervisor, your manager? Can you give us some more explanation about how things were done or decided?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both the management and the dispatchers, but I guess they were receiving their instructions from a higher level, from the Minister of the Interior perhaps. Based on these instructions, or, rather, approval, they conveyed to us instructions to go out because it was sort of safe. But you never knew how safe it was, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you personally received guide-lines from your direct supervisor, or how was it done in practical terms? Would you go to work? And then how did you learn whether the trams were going to run or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just slowly. I will first answer your first question. You asked me if I went to work. We all went to work everyday, gathered together in the morning, and then we would know whether it was safe or not. Whether it was the manager or whoever that had received instructions, we did come everyday and we sat there in the depot waiting for permission to leave and go out. I just forgot what your second question was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: That was my question, precisely. Thank you for this answer. Now, regarding the 27th of February, what time did you go to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We already had a schedule because a truce had been signed. I was in the morning shift on that day, so around 5.00 a.m. The morning shift normally went from 5.00 a.m. until 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And on which line were you assigned that day, for that morning shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was only one line. We just drove from the depot to Bascarsija. Now there's tram number 2, number 3, et cetera. There was only a single line from Bascarsija and back, and there were no others going to Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Here we heard a lot about the depot, and even I didn't ask where precisely this depot was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Alipasin Most there was a big depot and our head office. Would you like me to show it to you, approximately, if I can find it? That's one stop after Otoka. I don't know how to explain. And the name of the stop is GRAS.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We'll see with another witness, but it's Alipasin Most. The accident happened around noon or 12.15, and you said that you'd already been on the tram for a while. Was this situation normal before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was peaceful throughout. I drove on. I was nearing the end of my shift. It was just towards the end of my shift, and I was supposed to be handing over soon after.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like my assistant to show document 428, a 65 ter document. Second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, can you read English?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a little.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's see the first page of that document. Could we have a close-up of this first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, this is a report. You mentioned UNPROFOR. You said that UNPROFOR was there, and in fact they were very close to where the accident took place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, Madam Witness, when we had this discussion, you said you didn't know if they were ABiH units, but you did say that they were UNPROFOR units. Do you remember some 15 minutes ago we discussed that topic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember what I said. I tried to explain a while ago that in that section of Marindvor there were several UNPROFOR vehicles. They were usually parked there. I'm not saying they had any kind of headquarters there. They would just park there and they would take turns.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Every day UNPROFOR reported about the situation in Sarajevo. We have this report on what happened on April 27, 1995. This report was issued at half past 11.00 in the evening, after the incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at the picture. Can we see it on the screen, please, the cover page of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In this report your tram is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the interpreters' assistance, there is a sentence where it's indicated that four people were wounded on the tram in Sarajevo. We can see it on the screen where the number 4 appears. Let's now move on to page 2 of that document. There's a paragraph entitled "Faction Activity." Here, there are a few words about the Sarajevo sector, or area. Thank you, yes. Here you'll see number 8 in the paragraph. Once again, with the interpreters' assistance, please read what's written from number 8 onwards, because I don't want to translate myself. So with the interpreters' assistance, Your Honour, could we ask the interpreters to translate that particular sentence for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Does counsel want this read out in English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The sentence beginning "It..."?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The sentence beginning "It..." would you please translate that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Eight times SA rounds were fired at a tram near the Holiday Inn (BP 910593) injuring four (not confirmed) people."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We do have a B/C/S translation, so we can provide the witness with that. Have you read it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, she has read it. What's the question now? We do need to make some progress, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, could this reference relate to your tram?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on this, somehow it doesn't strike me as my tram, because here it says that -- just a second, please. There was something here that I wasn't quite clear about. It says a fire-fight between both factions occurred at the same time near the Holiday Inn hotel. The Holiday Inn is further up. Four injured from the Vrbanja bridge. Can't be. Vrbanja is over there and the Holiday Inn and my incident was further down near the Marshal Tito barracks. I'm not sure how they put this together.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: According to you, this wouldn't be your tram, then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It can't possibly be my tram. This is a different thing altogether there. This is the Holiday Inn. Unless they see this as a single section and they call it the Holiday Inn. But this seems to be a reference to a different incident, and I have no idea what they're referring to here. I can't say whether this is true or not, but this is certainly not what happened to me. I know what happened to me, and this is not it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What happened near the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what happened there. On that day, the only thing that happened was my incident. But before that time there were many people who were getting hurt all the time near the Holiday Inn, which was known to be a dangerous area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But did your incident happen near the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, quite near. This could be a reference to my incident, if that's what they choose to call it. But if you want accurate information on what happened and where, then this can't be it. For example, they say that this occurred near the Holiday Inn. That could be read as a reference to my incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the English text, I don't see the Holiday Inn mentioned. Is it there? Yes, it's there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I find confusing. Because what it says is, "near the Holiday Inn." That's what I find confusing. To some extent -- well, it is in the vicinity of the Holiday Inn. That's if they see that entire area as one section, one neighbour, Marindvor and Holiday Inn together. And it says that a fire-fight between both factions occurred at the same time. I don't know if a fire-fight actually occurred between two different factions. As far as I know, they, the other side, were firing at us. That's all I know, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, you're a bit surprised but what is written here, but maybe you could not see the shooting that was taking place towards the Serb-held territory. You cannot be certain whether or not there were shootings, but, however, you cannot exclude the possibility that there may have been about an exchange of shooting between both warring factions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a second. You tend to put many question, Ms. Isailovic, and the first one was "You're a bit surprised at what is written here." Are you surprised at what is written here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not surprised. Why should I be surprised? This could be a reference to my incident if they think that they can refer to that as the Holiday Inn area, because sometimes the area is referred to like that. But we Sarajevans know exactly the names of each of the stops, so if you want to provide a more detailed explanation, you're likely to tell them something along the lines of, "near Marindvor, in the general Holiday Inn area."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, next question, and put the questions individually.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me that it may have been an exchange of fires between the two warring factions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot possibly agree because there is simply no way for me to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You're quite sure that the opposite is true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, could we have page 9 of this document, please, on the screen. Could you enlarge this a little bit, please, the fifth paragraph in particular. Not all the paragraphs are numbered. The last sentence, it reads as follows. There are a number of abbreviations in there. If the interpreters can assist us, please. At 8, mention is made of the cease-fire. Could this sentence be translated, please, be translated into B/C/S for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters don't know which sentence. The usual practice is that somebody in the courtroom reads it out and then it is interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the sentence that you --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last sentence in the fifth paragraph which starts with "The tram travelling between ..." and it's the last sentence in that paragraph, which reads "EMG CF 8 has been attributed to the BSA," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're waiting for that translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has been translated. I have been reading this in English, so assume it has been translated into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is this document, Ms. Isailovic? What is its source?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have seen the first page of this document. This is a report, a situation report, of the 26th of February, 1995. This is addressed to the UNPROFOR command in Zagreb and was sent by the command or commander of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Can the screen go back to the sentence that was just translated. And "MGCFV," how are we to know what that means?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you like, we can ask the question of Mr. Fraser who will be heard also. In light of the document, "cease-fire violation," I think that's what it stands for. But perhaps we can wait and put this question to this other witness who will be called to testify. This was my last question before offering this document as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So I note we're going to have Mr. Fraser. But do you know what "MG" means? You gave us "CFV" as "cease-fire violation."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't smart enough to know what it is, so maybe we can put the question to the witness when he comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To the witness? How would she -- would she know? I'm surprised.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness Mr. Fraser.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am setting this question aside for Mr. Fraser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Ms. Isailovic. Any re-examination, Ms. Marcus?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit the document. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D41, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, two short last questions. When I was questioning you earlier, you circled an area on both the map and the photograph which you identified as the area you believe the shots came from. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Learned counsel from the Defence showed us a document describing an incident where the origin of fire was the Vrbanja bridge and the red building. Is the Vrbanja bridge and the red building included in the area that you circled as origin of fire for your incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Vrbanja is further up, up the - what's it called? - what the Defence said. Vrbanja is further up, and the area where the shots that were fired at my tram came from is further down. That's Grbavica. Vrbanja is a different thing altogether and Grbavica is something completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much further up? What is the distance that Vrbanja is from the place where your incident took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult to be specific. If, in this document, they believed -- they believed the Holiday Inn to be the same thing as the Marshal Tito barracks, then maybe they might believe that Vrbanja and Grbavica are the same thing, although in reality these are two different areas, two different municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, before the shots began at your tram, before you heard the first shots, did you hear any shooting of any kind on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-118 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was really quite peaceful. I was happy that I was about to get off work and hand over, so I heard nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, you said Vrbanja is a different municipality from the area in which your incident took place. I had asked you to give an approximation of the distance between the two places. Can you try to give us an idea of the distance between Vrbanja and the place where your incident took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The distance is not really that great. Vrbanja is sort of near Grbavica. There isn't that much of a distance. It's on the same side. Vrbanja or Grbavica, both were under the control of the Serb army. It was just before Marindvor and across the river at Miljacka, and then over there everything was under their control. Whether it was Vrbanja or Grbavica, it doesn't really make that much of a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next witness, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Witness 26, Alma Cehajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Ms. Marcus

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name and your date of birth for the Court.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Alma Mulosmanovic. I was born on the 24th of April, 1976, in Sarajevo. Did I skip anything?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, can we just clarify your name. We have two statements from you. Your 1996 statement has your surname as "Cehagic" and your 2006 statement refers to you as "Cehajic-Mulosmanovic." Can you please clarify for us what is your correct surname.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I got married in 2002 and I changed my last name to Mulosmanovic. Before my last name was Cehajic. So in the first statement, it should be J instead of G; it was Cehajic and not Cehagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. How long have you lived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was born. My parents were born there, too, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note that we are approaching the break time. This might be a good place to stop, but I leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, did you give a statement to Tribunal investigators on the 22nd of February, 1996?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What language did you give that statement in, please?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mainly in Bosnian, and some supplemental information was provided in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you re-read that statement before coming to court?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you give another statement to Tribunal investigators on the 20th of March, 2006?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I'm not sure about the date. But, yes, I did give a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What language did you give that statement in?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Also in Bosnian and in English as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you re-read that statement before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Is there anything that you would like to clarify or correct now from either of your statements?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing in particular, except that in the statement I said that I went to see an optician and to my university classes and I also went to a dentist's clinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I request the court officer, please, to call up 65 ter number 2897, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, in just a moment on your monitor you should see a page of your statement which I believe is the line that you are referring to, and so you could clarify for us what you'd like to change. Do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But just give me a moment, please. So that's second line from the top. I was on my way back from being at school and the optician and the dentist.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. With this addition that you just made now and with the correction of your name that you just clarified for us before, would you say that these two statements that you've given are a true and accurate representation of what you told Tribunal investigators on the 22nd of February, 1996, and the 20th of March, 2006?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions today, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I would like to request that these two statements be given exhibit numbers. They have already been admitted pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: These will be admitted as Exhibit P178, the statement of 22nd February, 1996; and Exhibit P179, the statement dated 20th March, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I now request the court officer to pull up 65 ter number 2872.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: While that is loading, Madam Witness, your evidence given in those two statements relates to an incident in which a tram you were riding on was fired upon. Can you tell the Court the date of that incident, please.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The 27th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: From which part of town was the tram coming?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was moving from the direction of Bascarsija.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And in which direction was the tram heading?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was heading to Cengic Vila, that is to say, towards the west.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Where was the tram when the shooting began?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately at the intersection where the museum and the Marshal Tito barracks were. However, since the tram was moving, I cannot give you the precise location. But this is more or less where it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Which direction were you facing while you were on the tram?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was facing the Marshal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you standing or were you sitting?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you remember from which direction the shots came?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The shots came from behind me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, what was at that location?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Behind me was the river Miljacka and the Grbavica and Vraca neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did the tram stop immediately when the shooting began, or did it continue?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The tram continued until the first shelter, the next shelter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: When you say "shelter," shelter from what, please?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a shelter from these two neighbourhoods, Grbavica and Vraca, if there was any possibility to find a cover. But we were safer behind this building.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, were you injured in this incident?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can we have the map zoomed a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, do you see the map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Would you be able to mark on this map with an X the approximate location where your tram was when the shooting began, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately this area here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And can you please draw a line along the path of the tram - you said the tram continued a bit - until the place where you remember, approximately, the tram stopping.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: So, roughly speaking, this is where it stopped, by the police station or these buildings. I think it's the faculty of natural sciences and maths.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you also indicate for the Court the approximate area where you believe the shots were fired from. Perhaps you could circle that area.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe a little bit to the back, like this. Like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'd like to have this map admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted. And the basis for her belief.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, can you tell the Court, please, on what do you base your belief that the shots were fired from the area you've just circled for us?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I had an entry and exit wound in my arm, since I -- my back was turned. There was an entry wound and then an exit wound, and I believe that had the shots come from nearby, we would have heard them. Had they come from a closer area, it would have been louder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you know who was in control of the area that you've circled as the area you believe the shots came from?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Chetniks or, that is to say, the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be admitted as Exhibit P180, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask the court officer now, please, to pull up 65 ter number 2914, and the court usher to please assist the witness in marking the photo as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, do you see the photo on the monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Would you be able to tell the Court from this photograph approximately where the tram was when the first shots were fired on the 27th of February, 1995? Perhaps you could mark it with an X as you did on the map.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately this area near this intersection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you now please draw a line from that location along the path the tram took until where it stopped, to your recollection.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is where it stopped, more or less. I'm not sure whether it went further on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you now please circle for the Court the area from which you believe the shots came.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, just one thing. Excuse me. I didn't see this line very well which indicates the river. I just wanted to encircle these high-rise buildings all together. Yes, here. This is where the river is, and this -- that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. And the record will indicate that the witness intended also to circle the high-rise buildings in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And this will be admitted as Exhibit P181, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much to the court usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, could you tell the Court, what kind of injury did you sustain?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: That was an entry/exit wound. That was a light injury. The bullet passed through the muscle, slid down the bone and then exited.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you indicate on your body for the Court, please, where the entry wound was.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the record please indicate that the witness has pointed to her left elbow, on the front side.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And could you please indicate for the Court where the exit wound was.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the record please indicate that the witness has pointed further down on her elbow, on her lower arm.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers on the tram on the day of the incident?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing any of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you see any ABiH soldiers anywhere around the tram on the day of the incident?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing any ABiH vehicles anywhere near the tram on the day of the incident?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing any of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you remember any combat activity of any kind near the tram on the day of the incident?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, you identified the location from where you believe the shots came from as being under the control of the Serb army. Can you explain how you know that?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, everybody knew that, most of all because of the expelled population, so people testified to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall what the weather was like on the 27th of February, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was cloudy. There was no rain or snow, but it was cloudy. I remember that because I had my umbrella with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was the tram crowded?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was pretty crowded.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you were wearing on that way?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was wearing a light purple jacket, blue jeans, Adidas tennis shoes, and a green blouse and a green umbrella.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was the area that you were travelling through when the tram came under fire, was it known to be a dangerous area?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Each area was dangerous, more or less. This particular area was dangerous. Every intersection was dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Why was this intersection known to be a dangerous area?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Because it was an open space and in good view.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you clarify for the Court, "it was an open space and in good view" of what?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when I was travelling, you could see the high-rise buildings, the Vraca hills where the Chetnik positions were, although throughout the war any movement in any part of the town gave you an uneasy feeling, because you felt to be a target always. I always felt uneasy whenever I could see these positions. So these buildings at Grbavica were well visible, as well as those at Vraca.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Court the shots that were fired on the 27th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: First, we heard several shots. As soon as they hit the trams, we heard the first shots. We tried to lie down or to crouch. There was not enough space for me, so I just bent down, and the other people who couldn't find any space just lowered themselves on the steps of the tram.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened next.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: These moments seemed to last very long because all the time, just as all other passengers, I was just waiting to be hit. In that crouching position I just prayed to God, because shots were heard hitting the tram, that I wouldn't be hit in the spine or any such part that would leave me paralysed. Then I felt that I was shot in the arm. After I disembarked from the tram, I rolled up my sleeve and I saw that I had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you see anybody else injured on the tram on that day?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Not at this particular location, because I was right next to the door and I got off immediately as the tram stopped. A car took me to the first aid station, and another two persons were brought there as well, an elderly man and an elderly woman.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, how old were you when this incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Eighteen, almost 19.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How did this incident and your wartime experiences affect your life?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: This incident itself as well as the whole war and the suspense, whether you were going to be shot or not, whether you would be injured seriously or not, prevailed throughout the war. Wherever you were, moving out or sitting in your home, we could here the shots passing by throughout the war, including the shells. You could never know where they were going to land. They just whizzed by, and as soon as it passed it was a kind of relief. When I saw that I had sustained a slight injury, it was also a relief. But the worst thing was the moment of fear, or the fear that engulfed us throughout the war. Later on and after the war, I am still very tense. Before the war, not even as a child, I was not afraid of the thunder; however, after the war, I was woken up one night but some blasts and I ran to hide behind a cupboard. I don't know how long it lasted, until I eventually realised that this was just thunder, and then I went back to bed. I also had fears after the war while I was driving, which was not the case before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you been treated for this condition that you have? Have you seen a doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In physical terms, I was given assistance at the first aid station. My wound was dressed and I received an anti-tetanus shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I was talking about the, apparently, psychological damage that you might have suffered. Your fear of the thunder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't seek help from doctors. These fears kind of started to recede thanks to my faith in God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Madam Witness. My name is Branislava Isailovic. I'm an attorney-at-law, a member of the Paris Bar Association. I would like to ask you a few questions about the statements you made to the Office of the Prosecution. You will remember those statements because we discussed them a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We'll also talk about what you said a moment ago. You were shown two photographs, i.e., a map showing the streets of Sarajevo and a photograph. Although I can see this photograph on the screen - this is a 65 ter document, 2914 - I would like to discuss it with you further. You will agree with me that this is the photograph that you were shown a moment ago. You put some markings on that particular picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, please could you help the witness so that she can make some further drawings on the same picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago I think you made a mistake. You drew a circle which was a bit bigger than you wanted. I would like to go back to this. Could you please show us again the location where the shooting started, the shooting against the tram. Could you please mark this location with an X.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about this location, roughly speaking. The tram was moving. You want me to put an X there; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you can recall, the tram stopped close, that is, before the school of technology?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean it stopped before the shot came, or what? I don't remember where it stopped before the shot came.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The only thing you remember is the time when it happened. In your statement, you say that you were facing the Marshal Tito barracks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Marshal Tito barracks covers a large area. This area here, it appears to be empty, but actually that was part of the barracks. The barracks stretches all the way beyond the borders of this photograph. Probably the shooting started there and stopped there, simply because of the fact that the barracks covers a rather large area. I don't think I understood what your question was, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Madam Witness, have a better look. Here you have a work site, so to speak, you have an empty space just above the X or the little star that you drew on the photograph. Would you agree with me that this is the place where the Marshal Tito barracks was located?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was destroyed and now it's being rebuilt.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Let's assume that your tram was there at the cross. You indicate in your statement of February the 24th, 1996 - and you confirm it in the subsequent statement - you were facing the barracks, the Marshal Tito barracks, as you were on the tram.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was facing the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Let me, therefore, repeat my question: When the shooting started, you were still facing and you could see at that moment the Marshal Tito barracks. We've discussed that particular event with other witnesses. My aim, therefore, was just to determine where exactly the tram was when the shooting started. Now, the representative of the Office of the Prosecution asked you a few questions about the shooting and she asked you to describe the shooting, and you started by saying that there were a few shots and then people knelt down in the tram. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's true that we heard shots, and as soon as we did we tried to take shelter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened next? Did shooting continue?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were several shots, and the shooting continued until we reached our shelter. Later on, I can't remember whether the shooting continued or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: According to you, did the first shots also hit the tram? Did you hear a noise caused by a bullet hitting the tram?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before I was wounded, you could hear bullets impacting against the tram, blunt sounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And when you heard those first shots, did you hear them hitting the tram right away?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that there were bullets that were fired before, but I can't be 100 per cent certain.
