utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to go back to the photograph that's currently on the screen and where you've put this mark or star. Maybe we could assign a number to that particular star - number 1, for instance - to indicate where the shooting started for the tram. Let's put number 1 next to the X.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think it was behind the police station, but I'm not 100 per cent certain. There are several buildings there. There was another one over here that is quite like the other one, but you can't see it in the photograph. I'm not certain which. Today both these buildings belong to the police, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see exactly what you pointed at. Have you just pointed at the work site?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't show it now. I did say earlier -- well, roughly speaking, that it was in this area. But I can't decide whether it was behind this building or the other building that was very much like the first one. It's all in the same area, but I can't be certain. I really can't say. I can't put a number 1 there for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So that everything is clear, the second mark indicates the location where the tram took shelter; is that correct? To take shelter from the shooting.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Roughly speaking. I'm not sure. I said roughly speaking. I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: It's okay. Could you please put a little 1 just above the X, indicating the location where you first heard the shooting. There's an X or a star already on the picture. This is not really a cross. It looks more like a star. So just above that, please put a 1, and then put a 2 next to the place where the tram took shelter, please.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I'm telling you I'm not sure if it's this building or the other one. There is one right behind. You can't see it in the photograph. But it was in this area, roughly speaking. I'm not sure about the other one, because they're very, very much alike.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The photograph, for the transcript, and we know that you're not 100 per cent sure, but can you mark this with number 2. Could you draw a number 2 above that spot, please. Now, let me get back to this mistake you made a few moments ago. This is something you remember, I'm sure. You drew a larger circle on the photograph and then you rubbed it out, and you drew a line close to Miljacka. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to put an inverted question to you. The part you added on by mistake, between the route followed by the tram and Miljacka, is that part of the territory which was controlled by the ABiH army?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you see the trees in this photograph? These keep you from seeing the river or the area between the factions or parties. There's some greenery here and I'm not sure if it's to the south, to the west, or to the east. And there's is an alley there. It's probably to the north, actually. This is, roughly speaking, where it is. The line should be around here, where I drew this, where I drew the correction. But the buildings are high and they hide the line. You can't see it in the photograph because the buildings are in the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, the question which you are being asked is whether the part that you added on by mistake, between the route followed by the tram and Miljacka, whether that was part of the territory controlled by the ABiH army. What's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, there was a small patch that was there, but the buildings are very high so that -- well, it all looks mixed up in this photograph, if you include the buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, you haven't answered the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This area? Yes, yes. It was under the control of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, let me get back to these trees that prevent you from seeing properly. That's true. Are these evergreens, or what kind of trees are they? Are they always green, do they always have leaves on them, or does it depend on what time of the year we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it's mixed or not, but I think there are deciduous trees there, too. I can't be certain. I'm no expert on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you also talked about your life in Sarajevo. From what I understand, according to your statements, between 1994 and after 1994 you attended classes at the economic school in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And you moved about in town quite a lot at that time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the time, back in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time I was wounded, that was vacation time and that was exam time at university, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: After what?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: After the 27th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was moving about, yes. If I had known the war would take ten days, I would have hidden myself and I wouldn't have left home. But it wasn't safe inside the flat either. You had to go out eventually to fetch things. Some people stayed inside and some people ventured outside; it was just like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And as far as the tram is concerned, in your statements you indicate that it was very dangerous; nonetheless, you did get on the tram.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was dangerous all over the place. One of my friends died on her balcony which had a concrete wall just in front. So every place in town was dangerous. Nowhere was safe.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So can we agree that the war -- that there was an awful war being waged in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And can we agree that there were two warring factions?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if we go back to what you said about the shots a while ago, you said that the first shots, according to you, did not hit the tram. Do you think that these shots came from the territory controlled by the ABiH army?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I said I wasn't 100 per cent certain. I don't think they came from there. It was even the same sort of sound when the bullets were fired. There was no change at all to the sound, not in terms of the distance. This was several moments before the tram was hit; therefore, it's very difficult to determine. The tram was moving and the time lag between the two was very short. There wasn't much fighting going on or anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Firstly, I would like to tender this photograph as evidence. I would like the registrar to give it an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let that be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit D42, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to ask my case manager to display on the screen document number 428. This is document number D41.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm about to show you a document which is written in English. Are you conversant in English?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to have a translation. I do understand English, but I'm unable to testify in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. We will show you the first page of this document. This is a report that was addressed to UNPROFOR command in Zagreb, dated the 27th of February, 1995. This UNPROFOR report talks about the accident your tramway had. I have already tendered this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that the Prosecutor is on her feet. Maybe I should stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. This is maybe the fourth time that learned counsel for the Defence has referred to these incidents as an accident, and I would just like to clarify that that is not the way that the witness described it in her testimony, what her experiences were. She described it as an attack. So I would just like to object to the use of the word "accident" in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps she meant incident. She has not described an accident. So did you use the word accident?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. In French I did use the word "accident," but maybe I should be more careful. This event occurred and had adverse consequences; this is what I meant. In any case, we are talking about what happened so we can't qualify the attack or the defence beforehand or the condition in which this occurred. This happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're not to use the word "accident" because it's confusing and the witness has not described an accident.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall abide by what you have said.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So this discusses the events that occurred on the 27th of February, 1995. This is what we discussed a while ago. The tram was shot at, and you yourself were a passenger on that tram. Is the date correct? Do you agree with that date?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: There's a whole code next to the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This did happen on the 27th of February, 1995; is that right? The incident occurred on the 27th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know where I'm supposed to see the date. There are so many figures here. There is the date, "D27," the code "23308," February 25th, if that's what you mean. That's probably it, right next to that code over there. The whole thing is marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if we scroll the document up a little bit. We had the B/C/S translation on the screen a while ago. Unfortunately, we've been unable to find it. And I would like to ask our interpreters to translate the sentence that starts with "Shooting in Sarajevo, tram number 4," I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you have a translated version of this document in front of you now. This document is in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: "Four injured people on the tramway," I mentioned in this document, these people were shot at on the tram in Sarajevo. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me exactly where I'm supposed to look?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could learned counsel please just indicate exactly what page the witness is looking at, exactly which line, et cetera, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is on the first page of the document, i.e., where everything is indicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR acronym is on there, and at the end I think it says "Message."

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 1. Which line?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's page 3 in my copy. "Four injured in tram shooting."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This document and this UNPROFOR report, could it pertain to this incident in which you were injured, Witness?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Quite possible. I'm not sure if this report covers that whole day or not, but it's quite possible. I didn't write it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then if we move on to the second page of the same document, I would like this to come up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that in your translated version it starts with "Faction Activity." You can read -- there's letter A and it says "Sector Sarajevo." Do you see that? And then there is a sentence which starts off with the number 8. Could you read this in your own language, please.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, what exactly did you say? How does it begin?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: It says, "Eight times ..."

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have: "Eight times SA rounds were fired at a tram near the ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. Could you go on reading, please.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: "Eight times SA rounds were fired at a tram --" I'm sorry. "Eight times SA rounds were fired at a tram near the Holiday Inn (BP 910593) injuring four people (not confirmed). The origin is assessed as being in the Vrbanja bridge/red building area, where a fire-fight between both factions occurred at the same time."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This document is a very large document and the incident is described in three different places in this document - on page 2, on page 9, and on page 23. The portion that learned counsel has selected to put to the witness gives an unfair and inaccurate representation of the entirety of the report in terms of the -- the other sections of the report which clarify this incident. So I'd like to object to one small portion of the description of the incident in the report being put to the witness as an inaccurate representation of what the document says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can put that in re-examination, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just to make sure that I was trying to get as close to the truth as possible, I was about to talk about page 9 of this document, and this document, D41, is a 25-page document which we have tendered. Am I entitled to use part of the document - and I know that you do have the entire document - or have I violated the rules?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a matter for you. I mean, you put your case. You can put the part of, but if you know that there are other parts which relate to that incident, then, in my view, you should. But as I told Ms. Marcus, she can raise it in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, this is the last question I have concerning this document. Do you an agree with what happened on that day? There was an exchange of fire between the two warring factions in this area, Vrbanja bridge, Vrbanja Most, and the red building, which is Metalka, and Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't a witness to that, and I don't remember anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, what the UNPROFOR report mentions is this exchange of fire, and you were both a victim and witness to what happened.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about an exchange of fire. If they know about it, then it's all right. But I'm telling you what I know and what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One last question. A while ago you talked about this tram, and you said you could see Grbavica, Vraca and you said that that territory was to your left and to the left of the tramway. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that I could see it. I said, in general terms, that I had a bad feeling whenever I was within their field of vision, and at that moment I was in that field of vision but I was facing the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I was trying to speak in general terms. So, as a rule, if you follow the route of the tram which goes to Vraca and the direction of Ilidza, for instance, or Alipasin Most, there is an entire territory which is controlled by the Serbs, and you said that this was Grbavica and Vraca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo was surrounded from all sides on the hills, wherever you turned. But I felt more uneasy in this particular area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Is it because you knew that on other hilltops the ABiH army units were positioned?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, have you heard of Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. But I don't remember where the lines exactly there were, nor do I know precisely where Debelo Brdo is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know where Debelo Brdo is?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know Zuc?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that it's somewhere to the north with respect to the tram tracks, but how far exactly and what is the area that it covers, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And what about Mojmilo? Do you know Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I know where the Mojmilo neighbourhood is, but I don't know which part of the hill Mojmilo occupies. I cannot say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm putting all these questions to you because you've just said that on all the hilltops there were soldiers, and you've said in your statement that these soldiers were Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: We knew -- everybody knew that Sarajevo was surrounded. Whether this hill was closer or farther away from the town, I don't know. I don't know the precise names of the hills and how they are arranged, how far they stretch. But what I do know is that the whole of Sarajevo was surrounded and it was under siege.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that the hills all around Sarajevo were hills where the Chetniks were? Is that what you've been told?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say for sure for all the hills. We were surrounded, but where the positions were exactly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you were afraid. When you went past the hills, you were afraid. Do you think there were Chetniks everywhere?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, the hills were around. I moved around the town, not through the hills. And I could see from the windows of my flat a part of the Vraca hill, and I was afraid because a bullet entered my flat approximately from that area and I was afraid to be there. As for the other positions, I cannot say exactly where they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, precisely above Mount Vraca there is Debelo Brdo. That you know, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I know the name, but I don't remember any longer. I remember Vraca and I know that it was dangerous there, but I cannot tell you anything precisely about Debelo Brdo. And where the lines were exactly, I cannot say. I know that while I was moving about I was exposed from all directions. There were some buildings that offered cover from bullets. But as for shells, shells could have landed anywhere, so the entire area was dangerous. And I was afraid both in my house, which is in a relatively better protected area -- I mean in my flat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And where exactly was your flat?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Branka Blazek Street. That is in new Sarajevo, the municipality of Novo Sarajevo or new Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: What is that neighbourhood called, where that street lies? Because there are several neighbourhoods in Sarajevo, like Bistrik, Vratnik, Blace?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Malta, near the bakery.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can we agree and say that there were a lot of shots, a lot of fighting, between the two warring factions in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the entire Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I request the court officer to go to page 9. I see that D41 is still displayed. If I could request page 9, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, do you have page 9 in the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Would it be possible for to us get the B/C/S version or is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a total of four pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there a page 9 in the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that in e-court the Prosecution only provided a three- or four-page translation. So it's not available in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, I'm going to slowly read a few lines from this page to you and, with the indulgence of the interpreters, we will translate them into B/C/S for you. "A tram travelling between BP 910593 and BP 907592 was fired at, reportedly resulting in one confirmed civilian casualty and possibly three other casualties. The confirmed casualty suffered a leg injury. The estimated origin of fire was BP 907589. Tramway service ceased following the incident. During the same time period both sides were involved in a fire-fight 300 metres away in the area of the Vrbanja bridge at BP 912589." Madam Witness, earlier you circled an area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the Defence counsel kindly switch off the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Defence counsel, please switch off your mic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, earlier you circled an area on both a map and a photograph in which you say -- you believe was the origin of fire. Do you recall doing that for us?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Vrbanja bridge is included in that circled area?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is nearby, but I'm not sure if I encircled it, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I request the court officer now to go to page 23 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I just ask what you mean by "nearby"? Can you give us an idea of the distance?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, could you assist the Court, if you have an idea of the distance between the Vrbanja bridge and the area where you were shot? Could you assist, if you are able to?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Vrbanja bridge separates a part of Grbavica, of the Grbavica neighbourhood, and this is where it ends. I circled the Grbavica neighbourhood. It is somewhat larger, and I said that I cannot give you a precise indication. Vrbanja Most is a kind of a borderline of the Grbavica neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you're not able to give a distance, whether it's 1 kilometre or 2 or 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a big distance, but I honestly can't tell you an accurate distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I possibly request the photo that we marked earlier, that's 65 ter number 2894, to be called up, and maybe the witness can indicate to us on the photograph if she knows where the Vrbanja bridge is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, are you able to locate on this map the Vrbanja bridge?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you please mark that location with a V for "Vrbanja," please.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could this photograph please be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P182, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I now ask the court officer to return to D41 and proceed to page 23 in that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a B/C/S version of that page, of page 23, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, I direct your attention, please, to paragraph (h) of that page. Would you be able to read that paragraph for us, Madam Witness, paragraph (h), that is.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: "Acting upon information from LOA BH at the UNMO HQ that a tram was shot at with three wounded civilians, UNMO patrol investigated alleged sniper fire against a tram in Sarajevo city at 271220A February 1995. The UNMO patrol confirmed that tram number 257, heading towards west, was hit by nine SA at GR BP 910593. The UNMO patrol observed only one spot of blood in the tram. The origin of fire was reported to be from south direction. After visiting State Hospital, BP 917596, and Kosevo Hospital, BP 923606, and also visiting local police stations, only one victim was confirmed, one female civilian who was hit in the left leg and received a fracture on the bone. During the UNMO patrol's visit to the hospital she was under operation and could not be visited until tomorrow morning. Allegations that one civilian car was hit by SA fire on the same place was not confirmed."

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, are you -- I'm calling your attention to the line that you read which says: "The origin of fire was reported to be from south direction." Can you confirm that the area you circled as the origin of fire is indeed from the south direction?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the south side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's leading. You can't lead in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Madam Witness, can you tell the Court, before the shooting began on that day, did you hear any combat activity anywhere around the tram?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: During that day, I heard what I confirmed, that shots were fired. I went about town and I don't remember. And -- excuse me, can I continue? It says here in the Sarajevo hospital, an elderly woman hit in the thigh and then an elderly man hit in the shoulder were admitted in the first aid station which was closest to the spot. The State Hospital was also close, but there was this first aid station as well and that is where I was taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I put a question to the witness for clarification. I would like the court officer to bring back the photo of the spots, I think it's 65 ter number 2894. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sorry, if I could just assist. I think it's 2194, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I took it from -- the quotation from yourself in the transcript. In any case, I would like to see the aerial photo that has been shown to us several times during this session. Thank you very much. Do you see the picture?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My question to you, Madam Witness, relates to the question brought up by President Robinson just a while ago; namely, relating to the strip of land north of the river up to the Tito barracks. On the picture you see there are some buildings in that strip of land. It's just north of the four high-rises on the other side of the river, the northern side of the river. The President's question to you a while ago was whether this strip of land was under BiH control, and you answered that question in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, beyond the river view from here, that is, to the north, it was under the control of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. Now, my question to you is, do you know or did you observe any military presence in that little strip of land? Were there any soldiers or military equipment in that area?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. There was a police station there and there is still one there, but I don't remember. I didn't pay attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Madam Witness, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for giving it. You may now leave. We'll take the break. We're adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I understand there was some mix-up with the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I apologise, it was our mistake. For various reasons having to do primarily with the health of a witness but other reasons as well, we changed the order yesterday to switch, but we neglected to inform everybody who needed to know, and we only realised that we had neglected to do that when we were about to call the next witness. So we have now -- we apologise for that mix-up, for that confusion. We've now reverted to the order that Your Honours expected and that the Defence expected, so the next witness is Witness 54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There was something I needed to address with respect to this witness before we begin. The witness is going to be handled by Mr. Sachdeva, but there are a couple of peculiar issues that I wanted to address with respect to this witness before beginning. I refer to the witness by his number because he has been granted protective measures. This witness is -- actually, I need to go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. President, I really have no reason to oppose the idea of starting with that witness. I'm prepared to cross-examine the witness. But if the witness's condition is really what the Prosecutor says it is, I wouldn't even mind having the other witness on the stand now. I could deal with that, too. If the witness is ill today and will feel better tomorrow, I wish him all the health in the world. It is, however, because of a matter of principle that it would be difficult for us to accept that change two minutes before the start of trial. If the witness's health is too poor for him to testify today, then how could he possibly testify tomorrow? I see no way for him to do that. If this is the sort of situation that we shall be facing in the future - I think we will often be facing situations that are inconvenient, to say the least - if the witness is in such a poor condition, it could be someone else testifying. But I won't be offering my interpretation today. I will be offering my true interpretation at another time before this Chamber. But this is very much a matter of principle. I won't be addressing that now. If you want me to address it, however, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, it's not clear to the Chamber, did you say that you are in a position to cross-examine the witness who is to testify now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one that was scheduled, yes, we're prepared for that one, for the next one and another five. That's not what I'm talking about. The schedule has been changed. The order of appearance has been changed with next to no time left on the clock. The one thing I have to tell you is this: This person appears to be in poor health --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you or are not prepared to cross-examine Witness 54 now? He is the witness who is now being brought by the Prosecution at late notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there's been a misunderstanding. Witness 54 was the one scheduled to begin, and we were prepared for that witness. Witness 144 was to be brought into the courtroom in order to testify before this witness that is scheduled, and that is what the problem is about, and that's why we oppose this. And I can say this openly now: I think this was done for tactical reasons, for purely tactical reasons, for that witness to be better proofed for the chief, after everything that we have heard from the previous witness. It is for that reason that, as a matter of principle, I must oppose this. I'm ready for Witness 144, and my learned friend has been ready for Witness 54 for a couple of days now. So that's what I'm talking about, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, I think I wasn't clear. Witness 54 is a witness who everybody expected to testify that we had -- that was on our list for days. We had intended to make a change yesterday. We didn't tell -- we forgot to tell you, so we're not going to make that change. So we have Witness 54 here, prepared to testimony, the witness that Mr. Tapuskovic is prepared -- we have gone back to the old order that everybody understood was going to be the order for today. And I have to say that I take some umbrage at the suggestion that we are doing this for some underhanded tactical reasons. That's a suggestion that really has no basis and is really uncalled for here. When we realised the mistake that we made, we went and we quickly changed it back to what they expected and we're prepared to proceed in that manner. And now I think these suggestions are unfair, and it's a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So Mr. Tapuskovic would have been prepared to cross-examine this witness from yesterday, Witness 54? Isn't that the position? Because he was originally down to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we will do our best to always be prepared for our next witness. I did not oppose that at first, when a minute before the witness's appearance, the Prosecution said there would be another witness. I, as chief counsel for the Defence, just couldn't agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. We'll hear Witness 54. I want to say that the hearing which the Chamber scheduled for tomorrow morning on the Prosecution's motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts will now take place on Monday morning, next Monday morning, not tomorrow morning. So we'll hear now the examination-in-chief of Witness 54. Let Witness 54 be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I'm being told by the court deputy that there's a request, which I thought would properly have come from you, for this witness's son to be brought in to be beside him in light of his condition. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I have not been involved in the proofing, but Mr. Sachdeva just shook his head at me, which indicates to me that we were not aware of it. His son is, of course, here and has been with him. I have never faced this situation before of having a family member in the courtroom. I don't see a problem with it myself. If Your Honours don't have a problem ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any comments on this from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None. None at all, Your Honour. I think this might prove helpful, after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's unusual, but the Chamber will allow it. But the son is not to sit immediately beside him. The son can sit somewhere else in the court; perhaps to the right of where the bench is. Maybe he will derive some comfort from sitting so close to you, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I love to keep everyone close to me. My one concern is, if he's seated over there, then one of the cameras might catch him and might deduce who the other person is who is taking the stand and thereby identify a protected victim. That is my only concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a very good [Realtime transcript read in error "God"] point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think the booth can be instructed not to show his face. They choose what gets broadcast, so I think they can handle that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that has been communicated to the booth. Let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you're in good fortune. It is reported that I said, "a very God point." Just a minor matter. It has that I said "a very God point" instead of "a very good point."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly thank you for it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness make the declaration. If he prefers to sit making the declaration, then he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you and to Your Honours. I just want to ensure that we are in private session currently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULOSMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you don't mind, I would like a short break, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a short break. I see we are very near the time for adjournment, so I think we might as well adjourn, it being 1.32. We'll adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
